Better Dividend Stock for Retirees: AT&T vs. Air Products and Chemicals ©Whitestudio2015 from Getty Images, Adam Simpson from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

AT&T yields 5% and plans to keep its dividend at $1.11 a share, while Air Products and Chemicals yields 2.3% and is still raising its dividend.

AT&T's dividend took a well-covered 44% of its free cash flow over the twelve months to Sept. 30, 2026, and the company guides free cash flow to $21 billion+ in 2028.

Air Products' dividend took 59% of its fiscal 2025 normalized EPS, but its dividend per share rose just 1.1% that year.

Two things to watch: AT&T's debt, which management expects back at its target only in 2029, and whether Air Products turns net cash flow positive in fiscal 2027 as it expects.

Any retiree living off dividends wants a check they can count on. And two big payers just gave very different answers about theirs.

On Oct. 21, AT&T (T:NYSE) said it plans to keep its annual dividend at $1.11 a share, a 5.0% yield, and put its rising free cash flow toward buybacks. Then on Nov. 5, Air Products and Chemicals (APD:NYSE) closed a fiscal year that CEO Eduardo Menezes said proved "we can turn the ship," and kept raising its dividend, which yields 2.3%.

So which is the better dividend stock for retirees: the bigger check, or the growing one?

Source: TIKR, at today's prices.

6 safe dividend stocks paying retirees 6%+ yields

There are over 100 stocks paying 6%+ annual dividends today.

But after an extensive investment review leveraging TIKR's proprietary data, we now believe only six of them are truly safe for retirees.

They're all yours for free as part of our new investment report, which you can access right here.

AT&T's check is staying put

AT&T's growth is in what it calls Advanced Connectivity: fiber, fixed wireless and postpaid phone. It added a record 769,000 Advanced Connectivity internet customers in the third quarter of 2026. Quarterly revenue rose 5.3% from a year earlier to $32.3 billion, even with Legacy revenue down 24.5%.

The dividend took a well-covered 44% of free cash flow over the twelve months to Sept. 30, 2026, and consensus has that ratio at 46% for fiscal 2026. Free cash flow has covered the dividend in every year since fiscal 2016:

AT&T (T): free cash flow vs. dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

Part of that cushion comes from a smaller dividend: AT&T paid $2.08 a share in fiscal 2020 and $1.11 in fiscal 2025.

Management plans to hold the $1.11 and buy back $24 billion+ of stock through 2028. The balance sheet is the weak spot, though. Net debt is 3.3x EBITDA, EBIT covers interest just 3.9x, and management doesn't expect leverage back at its 2.5x target until 2029, after its EchoStar spectrum purchase.

Good news for AT&T customers whose personal information was exposed in two data breaches in 2024: you are now covered by a $177 million class-action settlement. Customers who documented eligible financial losses from the breaches could receive as much as $5,000 for the first breach, while a separate class offers up to $2,500 for losses tied to the second incident.

There is, however, a significant catch: the deadline to file a claim has passed. Anyone who didn't submit one by Dec. 18, 2025, can no longer join the settlement. A federal court finally approved the agreement on October 2; meanwhile, AT&T denies any wrongdoing.

Take the First Step: FREE 2026 Investor Guide + Up to $25,000 in Silver with Qualifying Purchases

Why AT&T is Paying $177 Million

The settlement resolves lawsuits pertaining to two separate data incidents. On March 30, 2024, AT&T announced that a data set containing customer information had been released on the dark web. The exposed information included Social Security numbers and other personal details, per the official settlement website.

A second breach was then announced on July 12, 2024. Someone downloaded limited data from an AT&T workspace hosted on a third-party cloud platform, including phone numbers and records regarding calls and texts.

Customers sued, alleging AT&T failed to adequately protect their information. The cases were combined and settled without an admission of liability or wrongdoing.

Who Qualifies? Can You Still Try to File Past the Filing Date?

The first settlement class in the class-action suit covers people in the United States whose information was included in the March incident. The second class covers AT&T account owners, line users or end users whose information was involved in July.

Now, the claim deadline for this settlement was Dec. 18, 2025. Unfortunately, if you didn't submit a claim by that date, you cannot file now or receive a settlement payment in the future. There is no recourse; per Yahoo Finance, the claim period has permanently closed.

If you did file on time, be sure to visit the official AT&T Data Incident Settlement site for updates. The administrator states that valid claimants do not need to take further action while payment processing is pending.

How Much Money Could You Receive, and When?

The $5,000 maximum applies to first-class claimants who can document losses from 2019 or later and show they are traceable to the March breach. The second class allows up to $2,500 for documented losses from April 14, 2024, onward. People in both classes could quality under each, but must use separate documented losses.

title: AT&T vs. Verizon: Which Telecom Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
detail:
AT&T vs. Verizon: Which Telecom Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Robert Izquierdo, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 12:14 PM CST 5 min read
T
VZ
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

AT&T (NYSE:T) and Verizon Communications (NYSE:VZ) have spent years competing for the loyalty of American smartphone users and internet subscribers. Choosing between these two industry leaders depends on your outlook for infrastructure expansion and debt management through 2027.

AT&T focuses on a simplified business model emphasizing fiber and 5G deployment, while Verizon leverages its massive scale and global connectivity services. Both companies are navigating a capital-intensive industry where reliable network performance and consistent cash flow are the primary drivers of investor returns.

The case for AT&T

Within the landscape of communication stocks, AT&T has transitioned from a media conglomerate back to its roots in connectivity. It serves over 100 million retail wireless subscribers while aggressively expanding its fiber network to reach more homes and businesses. The company also manages FirstNet, a dedicated network for first responders, and is migrating older copper network users to modern high-speed alternatives.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $128.9 billion, representing growth of 3.5% compared to the prior year. Net income for this period was $13.1 billion, resulting in a net margin of 10.1%. This growth reflects steady progress in adding new wireless and fiber customers even as the company navigates a competitive pricing environment.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 1.6x, showing how much debt the conglomerate uses relative to its equity. The current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term debts with current assets, was 0.9x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached $19.4 billion, which is cash left after paying for operating costs and equipment.

The case for Verizon Communications

Verizon operates one of the largest wireless networks in the world, supporting approximately 147 million total retail connections. Its customer base includes nearly all of the Fortune 500 companies, highlighting its role in critical business infrastructure. Verizon recently strengthened its fiber capabilities through the acquisition of Frontier Communications and a multi-billion dollar artificial intelligence partnership with Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN).

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $139.4 billion, which is an increase of 1.4% over the previous twelve-month period. Net income for the company reached $16.4 billion, reflecting a net margin of 11.8%. Slower revenue growth compared to its peer reflects a highly mature wireless market where capturing new market share requires significant investment.

Key Takeaways

AT&T yields 5.2% and Coca-Cola yields 2.3%, but AT&T plans to keep its $1.11 dividend flat while Coca-Cola raised its dividend 5% in fiscal 2025.

AT&T's dividend took 44% of its free cash flow over the latest twelve months, against 79% for Coca-Cola.

Coca-Cola carries far less debt, and SpaceX's push into wireless is a new risk to the cash flow behind AT&T's dividend.

At today's pace, AT&T would pay more over 20 years, but Coca-Cola's yearly check would pass AT&T's around 2043.

AT&T (T:NYSE) shares fell 8% on Oct. 23 after Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is in talks for access to at least 80,000 cell sites to build a rival wireless network. Two weeks later, on Nov. 6, Coca-Cola (KO:NYSE) hit a record high while the broader market sold off.

AT&T's 5.2% yield is more than twice Coca-Cola's 2.3%. But over 20 years, what matters most is whether the check keeps coming and keeps growing.

So if I could hold only one for the next 20 years, which would it be?

Source: TIKR, Nov. 9, 2026. Payout ratios are for the twelve months to Sept. 30 (AT&T) and Oct. 2 (Coca-Cola).

AT&T's dividend is well covered, and stuck at $1.11

AT&T is growing where it's investing. Third-quarter revenue rose 5.3% from a year earlier to $32.3 billion, with a record 769,000 internet net adds across fiber and fixed wireless. On Oct. 21, it raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to around $2.40.

AT&T's free cash flow has covered its dividend in every year from fiscal 2016 to fiscal 2025:

AT&T (T): free cash flow vs. dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

Over the twelve months to Sept. 30, the dividend took a well-covered 44% of free cash flow. That leaves room for raises, but management would rather buy back stock. It plans to hold the dividend at $1.11 a share, down from $2.08 in fiscal 2020, while spending more than $24 billion on buybacks.

Debt is the weak spot. Net debt is 3.3x EBITDA over the latest twelve months, and management doesn't expect to get back to its 2.5x target until sometime in 2029. And on Oct. 8, SpaceX agreed to buy low-band spectrum to build Starlink Mobile into a nationwide carrier. CEO John Stankey's answer, on the third-quarter call: "the most durable customer combination in our industry is a fiber-fed broadband customer with a great wireless service on top of it, bar none."
